prompt: Two solid metal spheres, X and Y, are made of the same material. Sphere Y has twice the radius of sphere X. Explain why sphere Y reaches a higher terminal velocity in air than sphere X.
hints: How do volume (and weight) scale with radius?
How does cross-sectional area scale with radius?
solution: Weight is proportional to volume, which scales with radius cubed (r^3), whereas cross-sectional area (and drag at a given speed) scales with radius squared (r^2). Because sphere Y has twice the radius, its weight is 8 times larger while its area is only 4 times larger. Sphere Y has a larger weight-to-area ratio and must reach a higher speed before drag balances weight.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 1: Note that weight W is proportional to r^3 (since density is constant).
Step 2: Note that frontal area A is proportional to r^2.
Step 3: The ratio of weight to area (W/A) is proportional to r, so sphere Y has a greater weight per unit area.
Step 4: Drag per unit area must be greater to balance weight, requiring a higher terminal velocity.

mark_scheme.criterion: Weight is proportional to r^3 while cross-sectional area (or drag at a given speed) is proportional to r^2
Sphere Y has a larger ratio of weight to area, so it must fall at a higher speed before drag balances weight
